text: Nine years is long enough for a family to rearrange itself around an absence, and long enough for the son who left to believe he has outgrown the room he came from. The address is a flat in North London where four men — a father, his brother, two sons — have refined cohabitation into a standing quarrel with rules only they can hear. Into that the philosophy professor brings his wife. Peter Hall keeps everyone indoors and lets the talk do the damage: courtesies offered as bait, questions with a second edge, silences the whole room can price. It is funny, and the comedy is not warm. Across 111 minutes nothing leaves the flat, so nothing dissipates; every remark stays in the furniture. The wife is the only new variable in the arithmetic, and the four men work that out faster than her husband does.

Forty-three minutes, made in 1944, on what African-American soldiers were contributing to the war. The length declares the shape: too long for a newsreel, too short for a feature, built to be shown to an assembled room and talked about afterward. Stuart Heisler works part in record and part in dramatization, and the seam between the two is where the film gets interesting — documented service set beside staged scenes designed to make that service land with viewers inclined to resist it. A picture that has to argue its subject reveals what the argument was up against, and the pressure of the year sits in every decision about who speaks, in what register, and to whom. It is held in the National Film Registry. The forty-three minutes are still doing the job they were cut to do: presenting men in uniform to a country that had to be shown them.

Five crews, two days, and no way of knowing in advance which room the decision would happen in. Robert Drew put cameras with the President, with his brother the attorney general, with Governor George Wallace, with deputy attorney general Nicholas Katzenbach, and with Vivian Malone and James Hood, whose enrollment at the University of Alabama Wallace had promised to block in person. What comes back is a government talking to itself. How to move without handing the governor a crowd, how to act without making him a martyr for the segregationist side, who should stand in the doorway and at what hour. Fifty-two minutes, and much of it is waiting — the specific waiting of men who have already decided and are now choosing the moment. Malone and Hood wait differently. What is being timed over their heads is their own week.

The countryside is borrowed for an afternoon, and the boy taken out to see it knows the loan has an hour on it. Fourteen minutes, 1912: a poor child from the city gets a day in the open, and the day does exactly what such days do — shows him a life adjacent to his own, then ends. Harold M. Shaw films the outing plainly and saves his invention for what the boy makes of it, which is to imagine somewhere past the horizon where the return trip is not required. Early pictures used poverty as scenery all the time. This one stays with the narrower problem of a child who has now seen an alternative and is expected back by evening, and it treats his daydream as a piece of practical thinking rather than as a moral.

Someone had to sit in the cold until the animals stopped minding the camera. That patience is the substance of these seventy-one minutes: bison in herds, elk in their season, weather with nothing on the horizon to break it, gathered by James Algar's crews into a portrait of the continent's interior as it stood when the grazing herds were vast. The narration is of its decade and announces its meanings as it goes; the footage needs no such help. Animals keep their own pace, and the camera has agreed to that in advance. What holds the thing together is season and weather rather than story. It took the Academy Award for documentary feature, which in 1954 meant a wide audience sitting still for creatures with no interest whatever in being watched, and for grassland the film already speaks of in the past tense.

A traveling salesman comes home to a house that runs on money he has just stopped earning. Oklahoma in the 1920s, and the bankruptcy of Rubin Flood's company arrives in the kitchen before it arrives anywhere else: Cora counting what remains and letting the counting into the marriage, Reenie frightened of being taken out, a son kept close. When Reenie does go out it is with Sammy Golden, a Jewish boy with troubles of his own, which puts a second pressure into a town that has its opinions ready-made. Delbert Mann gives it 124 minutes and stages it almost entirely in rooms, so the arguments are never about their stated subject — a bill, a dance, an evening spent elsewhere — and the worst thing said in that house has been rehearsed for years before anyone says it aloud.

The tunnel had to be lit before it could be photographed, so a work car strung with lamps ran the parallel track, keeping pace. Billy Bitzer rode the front of a train and followed another train through the dark from 14th Street at Union Square to the old Grand Central, a station of 1869 with eight years left before its replacement opened. The line itself was seven months old. Five minutes: columns pulsing past, stations arriving as slabs of light, the track ahead swallowing itself. On the platforms, people look at the camera the way people look at machinery nobody has explained to them yet. What survives is the ordinary speed of a new thing, caught before anyone had settled on how to feel about it, when riding underground was still worth the price of film.

A reporter invents a woman and prints her, and the invention takes. Marilyn David, a secretary who has been hurt by an already-engaged British aristocrat, wakes up as the No Girl — the one who turned down a title — because her friend Peter Dawes wrote the story out of a jealousy he will not admit to. Wesley Ruggles has eighty minutes and spends them on the machinery rather than the sighs: press manufactures a person, the person draws a crowd, the crowd converts into bookings. What gives the film its edge is the labor. Celebrity arrives as work with hours, and Marilyn has to perform a version of herself that a man wrote in an afternoon. Then Charles Gray comes back, as the aristocrat in a 1935 comedy always comes back, and she has two men and a fictional persona to reconcile.

He is known in the saloon, which in 1915 is a way of saying that people give him room. A wealthy woman who comes into the place is decent to him for a moment, and the decency does not take right away — the next thing he does is go out with a partner to enter a rich man's house at night, with the owner's wife asleep beyond the wall. Gilbert M. Anderson stages the burglary for suspense and gets it, but the live wire runs elsewhere: a man carrying an unfamiliar obligation into work that requires him to have none. Fifteen minutes is very little space for a change of heart, and the film does not pretend otherwise. It holds the arithmetic open — what one small kindness weighs against a night's earnings — for as long as it can.

Water, filmed close enough that it stops reading as water. Ralph Steiner spent twelve minutes of 1929 on the substance in its various states — moving, falling, held still — and cut the results to a rhythm rather than an argument. No people, no story, nothing being explained. What remains is pattern: light broken up and reassembled by movement, shapes that hold for a second and are replaced by their successors. A short film with a single subject either finds a hundred things inside it or runs dry by the third minute, and the interest here lies in watching a cameraman refuse to repeat himself using the least various material available. It sits now in the National Film Registry, an odd resting place for twelve minutes that represent no country and tell nobody anything.

Two narrations run at once and neither one yields. The first gives a life in more or less the order it happened; the second reels off words attached sometimes to the images, sometimes to the story, sometimes to nothing a listener can place. Under both, nine minutes of pictures clipped from magazines by Frank Mouris and laid down so densely that the eye cannot finish a frame before the next lands. Caroline Mouris directs an autobiography assembled entirely from other people's printed matter, which turns a personal history into an inventory of what happened to be lying around. The Academy Award for animated short followed. The prize is not why it holds up; the reason is that uncommon, physical sensation of being handed more than can be taken in, and enjoying the shortfall.

A hunting rifle drops to the floor, discharges, and the picture proceeds on two planes at once. Martha is laid in a bed with the congregation praying around it; an angel arrives for her; a road appears with a man called Judas Green on it, slick, working for the other side. Spencer Williams moves between the sickroom and the other world without machinery and without apology — each is as solid as the other, and the singing carries across the join. Fifty-seven minutes, 1941, and the economy is not a shortfall being covered for but the source of the directness: a moral geography laid out flat, the bedside and the road and the choice all within walking distance of each other. What people carry away is the temptation. What makes the temptation work is the room with the bed in it.

Gaby Brimmer wanted an education, and the film gives its length to the mechanics of getting one. A Mexican production shot in English, 110 minutes, following a woman whose body will not do what is asked of it through schooling, through the daily work of being understood at all, and through the ordinary business — friendship, wanting somebody — that films about disabled people are usually too solemn to permit. Luis Mandoki's attention goes to the arrangements. Who lifts her, who reads her, who stays in the house and for how long, and what a family builds around one person's refusal to be set aside. The Academy Award went to a supporting performance, which is the right place for it in a story where the person at the center depends on the people at the edges and knows exactly what that costs them.
